Chapter 11. Letting Go of Perfection and Embracing Progress.
Have you ever felt trapped chasing the idea of a perfect day, or wishing every outcome was flawless? You’re not alone. Perfection has this way of drawing us in—it promises certainty, success, maybe even a bit of control. But, honestly, that pursuit usually leaves us feeling frustrated, disappointed, and like we’ll never measure up.
Instead, what if we shifted our focus to something quieter, and much kinder? Progress. It’s not about getting everything right—it’s about moving forward, one messy step at a time.
Picture a new manager, eager to prove herself. She sets these sky-high standards, for both herself and her team. Every mistake feels like a disaster, and setbacks get blown way out of proportion. Eventually, the pressure just becomes too much. After opening up to her mentor, she decides to try something different. Instead of demanding perfection, she starts celebrating small wins and learning from slip-ups—encouraging her team to do the same.
The result? Everything shifts. People take more risks, creativity flows, and trust grows deeper. Suddenly, it’s not about being perfect—it’s about getting better together.
Or think about a college student who battles procrastination. Wanting to do everything perfectly, she ends up paralyzed—assignments get pushed off, and anxiety just keeps building. One day, she sets a timer for ten minutes and allows herself to work imperfectly. The results aren’t always neat, but the work gets done. And with each attempt, she discovers that progress matters so much more than perfection ever could.
Here’s something to pay attention to: most of us are way harder on ourselves than we’d ever be on a friend. That inner critic? It’s loud, always pointing out where we fall short. But learning to be gentle with yourself—to celebrate effort, to notice growth—can unlock a whole new freedom.
Letting go of perfection isn’t about lowering your standards. It’s about making space for creativity, for resilience, and for a real sense of joy.
Take the example of a busy parent, juggling work and family. The house feels chaotic, the to-do list never ends, and guilt is a constant shadow. But then, after a messy dinner—spilled milk, burnt toast—the family ends up laughing together at the table. And in that imperfect moment, the parent realizes: these are the memories that matter most.
So, if you take one thing away from this, let it be an invitation. Trade in the myth of perfection for the reality of progress. Notice those small steps forward. Be kind to yourself—and to others. Over time, embracing imperfection becomes its own kind of strength, opening doors to new possibilities you never imagined.
